messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Maya is a 21-year-old electrician apprentice who had been proud, before the crash, of how steady she was with her hands and how quickly she learned on job sites. The accident happened late in the afternoon when she was riding with a coworker to pick up materials. They were moving through an intersection on a green light when another car came through fast and hit the passenger side. Maya remembers the violent sideways jolt, the burst of shattered glass, and the sickening sight of another vehicle filling the window an instant before impact. Her body was thrown hard against the door and seat belt, and for a few moments afterward she could not tell whether the shaking in her arms meant she was badly hurt or only terrified. The other driver survived, but in the months that followed Maya could not shake the conviction that what happened had been deeply unfair, that her life had been split open by someone else’s recklessness and that nothing meaningful had been done about it.

In the weeks afterward, certain moments took on a charged quality that felt out of proportion even to her. Seeing roadside footage of cars crumpled after accidents, or even passing a fresh collision on the highway, brought back the visual impression of a vehicle suddenly rushing toward her door. Riding in a car with other people was especially difficult. She found herself bracing at intersections, watching the angle of approaching cars, and tensing when someone else had control of the wheel. Conversations about the future also became unexpectedly painful. When family asked about where she saw herself in a year, or whether she wanted to finish her certification and move out on her own, she felt herself go blank or irritable, as if being asked to imagine a future exposed something fragile and uncertain.

What frightened Maya most in those moments was not only the memory of the crash but what it seemed to prove about her. When she was trapped in a passenger seat or confronted with images of mangled cars, she had come to believe she could not trust herself to do the right thing if danger came again. The old confidence she had in her judgment felt gone. The shaking and weakness she remembered from the collision had also become evidence, in her mind, that her body was unreliable now, liable to freeze or fail when she needed it most. Even talking about future plans touched the same sore point: if she could be blindsided once and if her own reactions could not be counted on, then planning ahead felt naive. Each trigger seemed to confirm her sense that she was no longer someone dependable, physically or mentally, and that the unfairness of the crash was still hanging over her life unanswered.

Those beliefs, in turn, made the triggers spread into more corners of her day. On workdays, Maya sometimes had to ride with a journeyman electrician between sites, and she started dreading those trips long before they happened. Because she was certain she could not rely on herself or her body if something went wrong in traffic, every ride with others felt more dangerous than it objectively was. When coworkers casually talked over lunch about where they wanted to be in five years, she would withdraw or make a joke to end the conversation; in her mind, looking too far ahead invited the same kind of blindside, and she felt almost superstitious about it. The more unfair and unresolved the crash seemed, the more sharply she noticed accident scenes, dented bumpers, and news clips about collisions. Her attention kept finding reminders that other cars could come out of nowhere, and each reminder landed on the same conclusion that she was not safe with her own body or judgment.

Over months, this changed her life in ways that embarrassed her. She remained committed to the trade, but transportation became a quiet ordeal built into the work itself. She sometimes rearranged tasks to avoid riding with others, which drew comments from supervisors who saw her as less flexible than before. At home, she shut down conversations with her parents when they asked about saving money, future jobs, or whether she might want her own place. Being single had once felt incidental; now it fit with her retreat from imagining a life unfolding normally. She hated that her world seemed to narrow around traffic, accident images, and any demand to think ahead, yet she also felt these reactions were the only sensible response to what had happened.

Maya sought help after realizing that the dread was no longer fading with time. A recent ride to a job with two coworkers left her gripping the seat and silently scanning every intersection, and afterward she was shaken by how quickly her mind went back to the certainty that she would fail if anything happened. She says she wants to feel like herself again at work and to be able to hear ordinary talk about the future without feeling trapped. What she fears most is that the crash revealed something permanent—that her body cannot be trusted, that her judgment will fail at the worst moment, and that her life will keep organizing itself around one brutal, unfair afternoon.
